title: System Design Examples and Plans
description: Read 30 small design plans and browser models. Each example links to its lesson. JavaScript and SQLite models teach one idea; text plans describe systems to discuss or draw.

examples.title: Begin with the goal
examples.description: Plan a small school library service. Name the users, their main task, the data, and a clear goal before choosing any tools.
examples.code:
First version: school book search
Users: learners and one librarian
Input: part of a book title
Work: find matching books and their copies
Reply: titles and shelf labels
Goal: 95 of 100 searches finish within 2 seconds
Not included: payments or video lessons

examples.title: Requirements and tradeoffs
examples.description: Separate actions from quality goals. Compare two library plans, keep the rules that must hold, and write down a useful tradeoff.
examples.code:
Budget limit: 20 planning units per month
Plan A: one app, one database, cost 10 units
Plan B: two apps, database copies, cost 35 units
First choice: Plan A, if testing meets the speed goal
Accepted limit: app maintenance may pause the service
Revisit when: measured demand or uptime needs grow

examples.title: Follow one request
examples.description: Trace a book search from a browser to a service and database, then follow the reply back. Find where a slow step adds waiting time.
examples.code:
Browser -> Service: GET /v1/books?title=moon&limit=2
Service: check the title and limit
Service -> Database: find matching book records
Database -> Service: book 17, title Moon, shelf B2
Service -> Browser: 200 OK with the result list
Browser: show Moon on shelf B2

examples.title: Estimate demand
examples.description: Estimate searches per day and per second using simple numbers. Compare an average with a busy period and leave room for uncertainty.
examples.output:
daily searches: 3000
average per second: 0.14
busy per second: 2

examples.title: Latency and throughput
examples.description: Measure how long one request takes and how much work finishes. Use a small p95 example to notice slow replies that an average can hide.
examples.output:
p95: 130 ms
slowest: 600 ms
throughput: 20 requests/s

examples.title: APIs and contracts
examples.description: Design a small book-search API with clear inputs, replies, limits, and errors. Learn why both sides need the same contract.

examples.title: Choose the data
examples.description: Separate a book title from its physical copies. Use stable IDs and links to keep the library facts clear without repeating every detail.
examples.output:
Moon by Asha
copies: 2
203 on B2, 204 on B3

examples.title: SQL and NoSQL choices
examples.description: Compare tables, documents, and key-value storage using library tasks. Choose by needed reads, writes, and rules instead of a label.

examples.title: Indexes help find records
examples.description: Use a book index to understand database indexes. Create a small SQLite title index and learn why faster reads can cost space and write work.
examples.output:
id | title | shelf
17 | Moon | B2
18 | Moon | C1

examples.title: Transactions and safe updates
examples.description: Keep a book-copy claim and its loan record together. Use a small SQLite transaction and conditional update to prevent a second claim.

examples.title: Scaling up and out
examples.description: Compare one bigger server with several smaller servers. Use a tiny capacity model, then check the shared parts that may still slow the service.
examples.output:
1 server(s): 40 searches/s
2 server(s): 80 searches/s
3 server(s): 90 searches/s

examples.title: Load balancers
examples.description: Send requests across healthy servers with a load balancer. Trace round-robin routing and see why shared state and useful health checks matter.
examples.output:
request 1: A
request 2: C
request 3: A
request 4: C

examples.title: Caches keep useful copies
examples.description: Save a copy of a repeated answer in a cache. Trace a hit, a miss, and expiry, then decide which data can safely be a little old.
examples.output:
miss: Moon Book
hit: Moon Book
hit: Moon Book
miss: Moon and Stars

examples.title: CDNs and static files
examples.description: Use a content delivery network to bring public files closer to readers. Plan cache headers, versioned names, and safe rules for private responses.
examples.code:
PUBLIC COVER
Path: /covers/moon-cover-v1.webp
Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400
First request: edge miss -> origin -> edge -> reader
Later fresh request: edge hit -> reader

UPDATED COVER
Path: /covers/moon-cover-v2.webp
Update the page to use the new path.

PRIVATE BORROWING HISTORY
Cache-Control: private, no-store
Never place the response in a shared public cache.

examples.title: Copies improve availability
examples.description: Use replicas to keep extra data copies, then trace a delayed update and a failed leader. Learn why replicas still need backups and safe failover.
examples.code:
ASYNCHRONOUS COPY TRACE
Time 0: leader = 2; replica = 2
Time 1: leader records checkout; leader = 1
Time 2: leader replies "saved"; replica is still 2
Time 3: replica applies update; replica = 1

FAILOVER QUESTIONS
Which copy is up to date enough to become leader?
Who decides, and how is the old leader stopped from writing?
What data loss and recovery delay can the library accept?

examples.title: Partitioning data
examples.description: Split records across shards using a clear key. Trace a simple remainder rule, then check hot keys, cross-shard work, and the cost of moving data.
examples.output:
book 10: shard 1
book 11: shard 2
book 12: shard 0
book 13: shard 1

examples.title: Consistency describes agreement
examples.description: Compare fresh and delayed reads across copies. Use a book checkout to explain consistency promises and the choices made during a network break.
examples.code:
ONE BOOK COPY, TWO DESKS
Start: A and B both show "available".
A saves checkout and confirms success.
B has not received that change yet.

Eventual read at B: may still show "available".
Strong read after success: must show the checkout or a newer state.

DURING A BROKEN LINK
Option 1: delay or refuse work that cannot keep the strong promise.
Option 2: let separated parts answer, allowing old/conflicting states.
Choose a rule for each action, and plan how conflicts are resolved.

examples.title: Queues handle work later
examples.description: Put slow jobs in a queue and let workers finish them later. Count a growing backlog, then plan acknowledgments, duplicate jobs, and failure handling.
examples.output:
round 1: 2 waiting
round 2: 4 waiting
round 3: 6 waiting
round 4: 8 waiting

examples.title: Retries need safe rules
examples.description: Retry a temporary failure with limits and increasing delays. Use stable request IDs so a lost reply does not repeat an important action.
examples.output:
retry 1: wait 120 ms
retry 2: wait 205 ms
retry 3: wait 430 ms

examples.title: Timeouts and circuit breakers
examples.description: Limit waiting with timeouts and pause calls to a failing service with a circuit breaker. Trace closed, open, and half-open states using a small model.

examples.title: Rate limits and backpressure
examples.description: Keep a busy service from taking too much work. Compare a request limit with a signal to slow down, then trace a small JavaScript model.

examples.title: Backups and recovery
examples.description: Plan how to recover lost data. Tell backups from replicas, set simple recovery targets, and practise restoring a safe copy.
examples.code:
Practice recovery plan
Important facts: book copies and current loans
Backup schedule: one backup each hour
Separate copy: stored away from the live database
Allowed lost changes (RPO): at most 60 minutes
Target time to restore (RTO): at most 30 minutes

Example drill
12:00 - data point saved by the last good backup
12:40 - the practice database is damaged
12:55 - restore and checks finish
Gap since backup: 40 minutes
Time to restore: 15 minutes
Result: both targets met in this drill

examples.title: Observe and review the design
examples.description: Use metrics, logs, and traces to understand a service. Check a small error-rate calculation, then review a design with clear evidence.
examples.output:
requests: 5
failures: 1
error percent: 20
successful average ms: 100

examples.title: Security and privacy in a design
examples.description: Protect private facts at each boundary. Learn identity checks, permissions, safe inputs, and why a design should collect only the data it needs.
examples.code:
Loan-history design boundary
Public: book titles and shelf locations
Private: which reader borrowed which copy

Request: GET /readers/me/loans
1. Use HTTPS for the connection.
2. The service checks the caller's identity.
3. The service checks permission to read these loans.
4. Read only this reader's permitted loan records.
5. Return only fields needed by the screen.

Log: request r52, action=list-loans, result=allowed
Do not log: password, access token, full loan history
Storage rule: keep records only as long as the policy needs

examples.title: One app or several services?
examples.description: Compare one application with several services. Keep clear module boundaries, then decide when a separate service is worth its extra work.
examples.code:
One app, clear internal jobs
Library application
  Catalog module: book titles and copies
  Loan module: borrow and return rules
  Reminder module: overdue reminder jobs

First version
One application deployment
One database with clear table ownership
One queue for reminders

Possible later split
Reminder service owns reminder jobs
Loan module publishes LoanCreated events
Reminder service can be unavailable while borrowing still works
Events may repeat: the reminder service must handle duplicates

examples.title: Design a school library service
examples.description: Plan book search, borrowing, and returns for a small library. Follow one safe loan and explain what happens when two readers want the same copy.
examples.code:
School library: one small service and one database
GET /books?title=moon -> matching public book details
POST /loans {copyId, requestId} -> saved loan or clear refusal
POST /loans/{loanId}/return -> returned loan or already returned

Borrow one copy
1. Check the reader and their permission to borrow.
2. Begin a transaction and claim the unique reader/requestId.
3. For an already saved request, check the details and return its result.
4. For a new request, change Copy.state to on-loan only if still available.
5. If a copy changed, add the Loan; otherwise prepare a refusal.
6. Save that outcome for this requestId and commit together, then reply.
7. Concurrent requests with the same ID wait or retry; do not execute twice.

Rule: a physical copy has at most one current loan.
Reminder failure must not undo a saved loan.

examples.title: Design a URL shortener
examples.description: Plan a service that turns a long web address into a short link. Handle code collisions, redirects, expired links, and unsafe destinations.
examples.code:
Short-link design
POST /links {destination} -> {code, shortUrl}
GET /s/{code} -> temporary redirect or not-found reply

Link record
code: unique short label
destination: checked HTTP or HTTPS web address
createdAt, expiresAt, disabledAt

Create
Check address and creation limits.
Generate an unpredictable candidate code.
Insert only if the code is unused; retry a bounded number of collisions.

Open
Look up the code.
Check disabled/expired state.
Reply with HTTP 302 and the checked destination.
Unknown, expired, or disabled code -> clear unavailable page.

examples.title: Design a small chat app
examples.description: Plan saved messages and live delivery for a small chat. Handle repeated sends, missing connections, message order, and private group access.
examples.code:
Small group-chat design
Conversation: conversationId, name
Member: conversationId, readerId
Message: messageId, conversationId, senderId, clientMessageId, sequence, text

Send {conversationId, clientMessageId, text}
1. Check the sender's identity and current membership.
2. Save the message once for this sender/clientMessageId in the conversation.
3. Assign its next sequence number within the conversation.
4. Save a delivery-event record with the message, then commit.
5. Tell the sender the message is saved.
6. Send live updates to connected permitted members.

Reconnect {conversationId, afterSequence}
Check membership, then return saved messages after that sequence in order.
Receivers ignore repeated messageIds.

examples.title: Design a news feed
examples.description: Build a small feed of recent posts. Compare making the feed when it is read with preparing it when a post is written, and protect private posts.
examples.code:
Small club-news feed: build on read first
Post: postId, authorId, createdAt, text, visibility, deletedAt
Follow: readerId, authorId

POST /posts -> save one checked post
GET /feed?cursor=... -> up to 20 permitted recent posts

Read flow
1. Check the reader and current follow list.
2. Find recent posts from followed authors.
3. Remove deleted posts and posts the reader may not see.
4. Sort newest first by createdAt, then postId to break ties.
5. Return 20 posts and a cursor for the next page.

Later option: precompute lists of post IDs for ordinary accounts.
Popular authors may still be combined at read time.
Recheck current permission before returning private post content.

examples.title: Design a file-upload service
examples.description: Plan a private file upload without sending large files through every app server. Track upload states, check the stored bytes, and clean up failed work.
examples.code:
Private file-upload design
File: fileId, ownerId, storageKey, storedVersion, size, status
States: waiting -> uploaded -> checking -> ready (or rejected)

POST /uploads {name, expectedSize, type}
  Check caller and allowed size; reserve quota with the waiting record.
  Create a new private temporary key and a short-lived upload grant.

Browser -> object storage: upload bytes to that allowed key
POST /uploads/{fileId}/complete
  Verify that bytes arrived; mark checking, not ready.

Worker
  Check actual size and type; scan the uploaded version.
  Copy approved bytes to an immutable private final key/version.
  Mark that exact checked version ready.

GET /files/{fileId}
  Check permission and ready state.
  Issue a short-lived download for the checked version only.
